items.title: Robotheca: an open catalogue of 475 buildable open-source robots, with ROS 2 support, URDFs and licences checked
items.summary: Hi all, I’m Klajdi. I’ve been building Robotheca , a free catalogue of open-source robots you can actually build, and the software around them. It’s still in beta, and before going further I’d love to hear from people who build robots for real. What’s there today 475 robots: arms, quadrupeds, humanoids, rovers, drones… 800+ robotics software projects and 75+ AI models For each robot: the CAD/STL files, the parts list (with prices when the creator gives them), the hardware and software licences, the build guide and difficulty, and tags like ROS 2 or URDF Licences are read from each project’s own files. When they’re unclear, the page says “Unknown” instead of guessing Every creator is credited and linked to their own repository What I’d love to know Is this useful to you? What’s good, what’s confusing, what’s missing? Which robots or packages should be there and aren’t? items.articleText: Can a social reflex stop a robot but never restart it? Testing a dual-dwell safety gate (Webots) - Projects - Open Robotics Discourse Can a social reflex stop a robot but never restart it? Testing a dual-dwell safety gate (Webots) Projects webots , safety marunigno-ship-it October 25, 2026, 3:59pm 1 Hi everyone, Following up on my earlier experiments with supervisory gates (Demo 8) : Webots Demo 8: Supervisory Gate Multi-Fault Lifecycle & Watchdog Hardening (QERRA-v2 Classical) I’ve built a new test to evaluate the recovery side of a safety event. My underlying vision in robotics is harmonious human-robot social collaboration —specifically in vulnerable spaces like hospitals or eldercare facilities & beyond. We want robots to react when someone calls for help or collapses. But here is the friction I constantly see: to make a robot socially aware, we have to rely on probabilistic AI models. If we let an uncertified perception model dictate the motor controllers, a lagging thread or hallucination can turn a 70 kg robot into a runaway hazard. I wanted to build a deterministic “floor” underneath the AI. The safety contract I wanted to test is simple: Perception can take away the permission to move, but it can never give it back. Before sharing the data, I want to be completely upfront. I am not a classically trained robotics engineer or a certified safety assessor. I am an independent solo developer in Greece, and I build this with AI coding tools (Claude, Gemini). I am sharing this here because I want to learn from those of you actually deploying robots around humans, and see if this architecture holds up. (If i ever get an answer! ). The Architecture: Doer-Checker I built a dual-channel pattern and tested it on a TIAGo base in Webots: The “Doer” (Navigation Brain) : An unprivileged process that proposes velocities (2.00 rad/s) over UDP. It has no direct access to the wheels. The “Checker” (Supervisory Gate) : A pure mathematical function step(state, params, inputs) → StepResult running on a strict 32 ms cycle. It is the only thing that writes to the actuators. The Reflex Layer (QERRA-HSR) : Evaluates distress. It enforces a 1.0s hysteresis dwell before it steps down from CRITICAL to CLEAR, preventing the robot from “chattering” if camera confidence fluctuates. The Latch : After any trip, the Gate requires the cause to be clear for a continuous 1.0s, followed by an explicit operator reset. The Run (14.0 Seconds, 438 Control Cycles) This is a single continuous simulation take. Times below are from the audit log. Sim time What happens Gate Response 0.03 s Boot TRIPPED (proposer not heard yet) 1.312 s Scripted reset Accepted → RUN at 2.00 rad/s 4.000 s Distress injected (0.85 conf), HSR CRITICAL TRIPPED on the same 32ms cycle (cycle 125), wheels clamped to 0.000 5.024 s Scripted reset while distress is active Refused (RESET_REJECTED_HAZARD) 7.008 s Injected distress removed Still TRIPPED 8.032 s HSR back to CLEAR (after 1.0s hysteresis dwell) Still TRIPPED, resets refused (RESET_REJECTED_NOT_READY) 9.056 s Reset on the first allowed cycle Accepted → RUN at 2.00 rad/s 14.016 s End of run, log closed Note: “Same cycle” means the wheel command went to 0.000 on the exact control cycle the status became CRITICAL. (Time spent computing the Gate decision in Python: p50 = 1.38 ms, max = 4.50 ms). A quick lesson learned: I initially predicted recovery at 8.2s. But there are actually two dwells stacking here: the reflex layer’s 1.0s dwell (to ensure the scene is calm), followed by the Gate’s own 1.0s internal safety dwell. The earliest reset possible was 9.03s. It was a great lesson in why writing down expected cycles before running is so important. Replay Audit Because the Gate is a pure function, every cycle is hash-chained into a JSONL log. Using an offline verifier (verify_log.py --replay), I fed the recorded inputs back through the function. All 438 cycles reproduced bit-for-bit with 0 execution divergences . (Head hash: eccb0d85416cf4a651205f34f3cc0d9275bff6e2b3baa512e4b23dbef0c2714a). (Transparency note: While the replay is deterministic, live UDP on Windows is not. An earlier take of this scenario tripped at 10.2s due to a host scheduling load that stalled the proposer for 160ms. The gate failed-closed exactly as designed). Honest Boundaries (What this does not show) No live detection. The 0.85 distress flag is a constant injected by my test script. Real CV detection (with false positives/negatives) is the hardest part, and is not tested here. No human in the loop. The resets are injected by a script to test the exact microsecond boundaries. Because of this, the video shows the robot auto-restarting after the dwells finish. In reality, a human must assess the scene before hitting that reset button. Not a certification claim. This is an independent simulation (Webots/Windows/Python), not an industrial RTOS. I am not affiliated with PAL Robotics. My Questions for the Community If you run robots in shared spaces (hospitals, retail): after a protective stop caused by a person, what is your actual restart rule? Remote confirmation? A physical button on the chassis? Is “perception may only stop the robot, but never start it” a contract you use in practice, or do you let perception modify trajectories directly inside the safety layer? In a real ROS 2 stack, I envision putting a node like this directly between the final cmd_vel mux and the base controller, blocking all other publishers. Has anyone implemented a strict latch-and-reset pattern this deep in the stack? What went wrong? Links: Video (31s, Webots window, unedited): Repository (Apache-2.0): GitHub - marunigno-ship-it/QERRA-v2-classical: Three-layer deterministic safety & ethical execution guard for autonomous robots (ROS 2 & Behavior Trees). Sub-ms physical reflex (QERRA-HSR) + moral filter (SEMEV-12) + values ranker (THRIVE). Fully auditable. · GitHub Evidence logs: QERRA-v2-classical/docs/demo9 at main · marunigno-ship-it/QERRA-v2-classical · GitHub Thank you for your time, and I welcome any brutal feedback you have on this architecture. items.title: Introducing Kimi K3.1 Pro
items.summary: Introducing Kimi K3.1 Pro Kimi K3.1 Pro landed on the Kimi API today - it's not yet open weights, but Moonshot promise "Full model weights will be released by Nov 4, 2026". They're also offering a "Highspeed" version that's 2-3x faster, at twice the price (except for input token cache hits, which are priced the same). The US dollar pricing is $2.00/million tokens for input and $10/million for output - the same as GPT-6.1 Sol and half the price of Claude Opus 5.5. Moonshot's own benchmarks show Kimi as approximately level with Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra - beating them on a few benchmarks, coming close on others. Artificial Analysis scored Kimi at 55 - ahead of Claude Fable 5.1, GPT-6 Astra, and Gemini 4 Argon (all at 53) and behind only Claude Opus 5.5 (58). This is the first time a (soon-to-be) open weight model has scored this highly against the frontier. I tried it out via the Moonshot API using the llm openai endpoint command I added to LLM 0.32 back in August: llm openai endpoint \ https://api.moonshot.ai/v1 \ --key kimi \ -m kimi-k3.1-pro \ "Generate an SVG of a pelican riding a bicycle" \ --responses \ -o reasoning_effort low \ > kimi-k3.1-pro-pelican-low.stdout.txt \ 2> kimi-k

items.title: A 10-year-old CNN outperforms frontier LLMs for skin cancer diagnosis
items.articleText: This is a melanoma. Figure 1. Invasive melanoma on the ear, under 0.8 mm thick. Both LLMs called it a seborrhoeic keratosis and said it could be discharged. The CNN called it a melanoma. Clinical photograph on the left, dermoscopic image on the right. Images: MILK10k , MILK study team, CC BY-NC. I showed these two images - a clinical photograph and a dermoscopic (skin microscope) image - to GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1, two of the most capable AI models available in October 2026. Both said it was a seborrhoeic keratosis, a harmless warty growth, and that the patient could be discharged. I then showed them to fine-tuned version of Inception v3, a convolutional neural network (CNN) first published by Google in 2015 and fine-tuned here on public dermatology images. The CNN got the right answer based on the dermoscopy view. It was one of 200 biopsy-proven lesions I gave to all three. The CNN named the right diagnosis (out of 6 possiblities) for 125 of them (62%). The two frontier LLMs named it for 84 and 85 (42%). A ten-year-old network, fine-tuned for about twenty minutes, beat both of them at recognising skin cancer. The test# The lesions come from MILK10k , a public dataset released through the International Skin Imaging Collaboration in 2025, in which each lesion is photographed twice: a clinical close-up and a dermoscopic image taken through the illuminated magnifying lens dermatologists use. I drew 200 lesions at random, all confirmed by histopathology: 100 that should not be discharged: 30 melanomas, 25 basal cell carcinomas, 25 squamous cell carcinomas (including Bowen’s disease) and 20 actinic keratoses. 100 that are safe to discharge: 50 benign naevi (moles) and 50 seborrhoeic keratoses. Every lesion was biopsied, including the benign ones, so these are harder to diagnose: a mole that somebody decided to cut out is one that worried a clinician. Basal cell carcinoma on the trunk of a 75-year-old man. All three models answered correctly. Invasive melanoma under 0.8 mm thick, with very little pigment. GPT-6 Astra called it a basal cell carcinoma with 95% confidence. Claude Fable 5.1 and the CNN called it a melanoma. Seborrhoeic keratosis on the leg. Both LLMs called it an actinic keratosis and the CNN a squamous cell carcinoma: all three were wrong, though all three would have kept it rather than discharge it. Figure 2. Three more of the 200 test lesions. Clinical photograph on the left, dermoscopic image on the right. Images: MILK10k , MILK study team, CC BY-NC. The LLMs were given both images and nothing else, and asked, as a clinician might use them, for the most likely of the six diagnoses (or “unsure”), a confidence, a second choice, and whether the lesion could be safely discharged with no treatment, biopsy or follow-up. Both models got the same prompt at default settings, and neither refused a case. The CNN is deliberately not state of the art. I used Inception v3 pretrained on everyday photographs and then fine-tuned all layers on 68,011 dermoscopic and clinical images from the ISIC Archive on a single H100 GPU. These 200 test lesions, and every other photograph of the same lesion or patient, were removed from its data (including the validation set) before training, so it had never seen them, and they were not used to choose the model or set its threshold. It scored both images of each lesion, combined them with most of the weight on the dermoscopic image, and chose from the same six diagnoses. You can try the CNN yourself . Remarkably the model is small enough to run entirely in a phone browser using WebGPU. Nothing is uploaded, and its random sample button draws from these same 200 lesions. Diagnosis: 62% against 42%# Figure 3. Correct first-choice diagnosis for the two LLMs and the CNN, which chose from the same six diagnoses. Labels show correct answers out of the number of lesions with that histology. The CNN was right more often overall and on most diagnoses. Allowing a second choice, it reached 173 of 200 against 134 and 138. It named 13 of the 30 melanomas against 8 and 11. The biggest gap was on the harmless lesions: it recognised 37 of 50 moles and 26 of 50 seborrhoeic keratoses, against 16 and 13 for GPT-6 Astra and 33 and 6 for Claude Fable 5.1. It was one short of GPT-6 Astra on basal cell carcinoma and behind both LLMs on actinic keratosis. The models also failed differently. Each LLM had a favourite answer: GPT-6 Astra called 75 lesions basal cell carcinoma when 25 were, including 14 of the 30 melanomas, and Claude Fable 5.1 called 53 lesions actinic keratosis when 20 were. The CNN’s errors on melanoma went the other way: of the 17 it got wrong, it called 8 a naevus and 6 a seborrhoeic keratosis. The results in one table# GPT-6 Astra Claude Fable 5.1 CNN (Inception v3) Correct diagnosis (of 200) 84 (42%) 85 (42%) 125 (62%) Correct in first or second choice 134 138 173 Melanoma as first choice (of 30) 8 11 13 Unsafe lesions kept (of 100) 97 96 77 at its preset threshold; 98 or 99 when matched Safe lesions discharged (of 100) 32 22 76 at its preset threshold Melanomas discharged (of 30) 3 4 18 at its preset threshold; 2 or 1 when matched Caveats# Small numbers. Two hundred lesions are enough to show the pattern but not to rank close results, and 30 melanomas give wide uncertainty on the figure that matters most. Each LLM case was run once; answers vary between runs. Hard cases. Every lesion was biopsied. On ordinary images from the archive the CNN separated lesions that should and should not be discharged far better (area under the ROC curve 0.96, against 0.86 here). Contamination. MILK10k has been public since 2025, so the LLMs could have seen it in training; if anything that would have helped them. The CNN certainly had not. Not state of the art. Inception v3 is a baseline. State of the art skin cancer diagnosis AI uses ensembles of images transformers trained on more data, and the regulated products built on them perform considerably better. Asked as a patient# Asked as a patient instead, with the clinical photograph alone and the question “do I need to see a doctor?”, both LLMs advised seeing a doctor in almost every case, harmless lesions included: for 99 and 98 of a further 100 biopsy-proven melanomas. Conclusion# A small, old, specialised network using an outdated architecture recognises skin lesions far better than two frontier LLMs. Run it yourself# The cases, prompts, every LLM reply and the scoring code are in one download , and the CNN is here . I designed the test and made the clinical rulings. The analysis and the first drafts were produced with Claude Code, Anthropic’s coding tool, which runs on a Claude model; one of the two LLMs tested is also Anthropic’s. Scoring was done by script against the histology. Images are from the MILK10k dataset (MILK study team, International Skin Imaging Collaboration), used under a CC BY-NC licence. Dr Magnus Lynch is a Consultant Dermatologist and Mohs Surgeon at Guy's Hospital and Honorary Reader (equivalent of Associate Professor) at King's College London. His clinical work covers skin cancer, Mohs and facial reconstructive surgery, and lasers; his research covers the cell biology of skin cancers and scars and the use of AI in dermatology. Full profile .

items.articleText:
## Security fixes

v2.1.0 fixes eight vulnerabilities in three servers. Upgrade
`@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem` and `@modelcontextprotocol/server-everything`
to 2.0.1, and `mcp-server-fetch` to 2026.10.24.

| Package | Affected | Fixed in |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem` | 1.0.0 through 2.0.0, and date versions through 2026.8.31 | 2.0.1 |
| `@modelcontextprotocol/server-everything` | 1.0.0 through 2.0.0, and date versions 2025.9.24 through 2026.8.31 | 2.0.1 |
| `mcp-server-fetch` | through 2026.10.19 | 2026.10.24 |

### `@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem` 2.0.1

* **Writes stay inside the directory that was checked** (Linux and macOS). A parent directory swapped for a symlink between the access check and the write can no longer redirect `write_file`, `edit_file`, `create_directory` or the `move_file` destination outside the allowed directories. **On Windows this is only partly fixed**; the advisory says what is still exposed and how to configure around it ([GHSA-53mr-w429-c597](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers/security/advisories/GHSA-53mr-w429-c597))
* **Paths are checked exactly as they are used.** The access check no longer strips a trailing quote or whitespace that the file operation keeps, so a sibling directory named after an allowed one with that suffix is no longer reachable ([GHSA-7rgq-gccq-qphx](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers/security/advisories/GHSA-7rgq-gccq-qphx))
* **A symlink spelled in a different letter case no longer passes the symlink check** for a new path on a case-insensitive volume, such as macOS's default. This was a regression in 2026.8.31 ([GHSA-4gxg-m5jx-9j57](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers/security/advisories/GHSA-4gxg-m5jx-9j57))
* **`list_directory_with_sizes` checks each entry before reading its size**, so a symlink inside an allowed directory no longer reveals the size and modification time of a file outside it ([GHSA-hhwq-wxfx-cj7g](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers/security/advisories/GHSA-hhwq-wxfx-cj7g))

### `@modelcontextprotocol/server-everything` 2.0.1

* **The HTTP and SSE transports refuse requests from other web origins.** They now check the `Origin` header and no longer send `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`, so a web page the user visits can no longer call the server's tools (such as `get-env`) or read their results ([GHSA-mvf5-2qqv-rg3c](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers/security/advisories/GHSA-mvf5-2qqv-rg3c))

### `mcp-server-fetch` 2026.10.24

* **The address check and the connection use the same host name.** For an internationalized (IDNA) host name, the server used to check one form of the name and connect to another, which could reach an internal address ([GHSA-v38p-wf49-hx2j](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers/security/advisories/GHSA-v38p-wf49-hx2j))
* **NAT64 addresses are judged by the IPv4 address they carry.** An address in `64:ff9b::/96` that wraps a private, loopback or link-local IPv4 address is now refused, as an IPv4-mapped one already was ([GHSA-66qx-2266-pmj6](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers/security/advisories/GHSA-66qx-2266-pmj6))
* **robots.txt is checked again after every redirect**, not only for the URL first requested ([GHSA-3jqg-r5pp-rmp2](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers/security/advisories/GHSA-3jqg-r5pp-rmp2))

### Upgrading from a date-versioned npm release

The TypeScript servers moved from date versions (2025.x, 2026.x) to semantic versions in 1.0.0. Package managers rank 2.0.1 below every 2025.x and 2026.x version, so they won't offer it as an upgrade. If you are on a date version, install 2.0.1 explicitly, for example `npm install @modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem@2.0.1`.

## Speech

Ollama can now generate [speech](https://docs.ollama.com/capabilities/speech) on macOS. `ollama run` plays text or a chat model's reply aloud as the audio is generated, and apps can stream audio through the OpenAI-compatible `/v1/audio/speech` endpoint.

```sh
ollama run phonon "Hello from Ollama."
```

## d3 decision models

[d3](https://ollama.com/library/d3) brings vLLM Semantic Router's decision models to Ollama. Give a model text, structured state, or an image, and ask it to classify, answer yes or no, or score options with probabilities. The family includes 2B, 4B, 9B, and 27B sizes.

```sh
ollama run d3 "A customer says their card was charged twice." --ask "Is this a billing issue?"
```

Using onboard visual feedback, the humanoid demonstrates pushing objects weighing up to 35 kilograms and lifting objects up to 20 kg to arrange the letters “KAIST.” [ KAIST DRCD Lab ] When you don’t spend any money on sensors for your robots, you can afford much bigger wheels. items.title: Teradyne Robotics partners with Sereact to scale physical AI in retail and logistics
items.summary: Sereact and Teradyne have already shipped hundreds of UR robots in dual-arm systems to live customer sites across Europe. The post Teradyne Robotics partners with Sereact to scale physical AI in retail and logistics appeared first on The Robot Report .
items.articleText: At Zalando’s fulfillment centers in Germany and Poland, Sereact and Universal Robots now autonomously processes returned fashion items. | Source: Teradyne Robotics Teradyne Robotics, the company behind Universal Robots and Mobile Industrial Robots, last week partnered with Sereact. The companies aim to accelerate industrial AI solutions in retail, logistics and manufacturing. Through this partnership, Sereact’s Cortex physical AI platform runs robot arms from Universal Robots to give retailers and logistics providers a proven way to automate unstructured tasks such as returns handling and piece picking. Together, the companies have already shipped hundreds of UR robots in dual-arm systems to live customer sites across Europe . “Physical AI only matters when it performs in real-world operations, and that is where Universal Robots has always been at home,” said Jacob Pascual Pape, the chief commercial officer of Teradyne Robotics . “Our robots are built for the AI era: open, connected, and proven through more than 100,000 industrial deployments. That is why Sereact has chosen our platform.” “When combined with Sereact’s Cortex, the joint solution handles mixed goods, unknown items, and varied packaging,” he added. “This has moved well beyond the demo or pilot stage with the technology now usefully deployed at real customer sites. Our technologies are a natural fit and through our partnership we will scale these AI-powered solutions fast across applications, industries and markets.” To serve the rapidly growing demand and bring the joint solution to North America, Sereact this summer opened U.S. headquarters in Charlestown, Mass. The company develops physical AI software that enables robots to grasp, identify, and handle objects they have never seen before. The companies made the announcement at NVIDIA GTC Berlin 2026. Teradyne and Sereact already have deployments running Teradyne Robotics and Sereact said their joint offering can help a variety of critical logistics and manufacturing use cases. These include piece picking and sortation, order induction, machine tending, bin consolidation, kitting, packing, and goods handling. “Returns, replenishment, kitting — with Cortex, every one of these applications runs on the same production model. One brain serves every robot, with no retraining for each new item or task. And what one robot learns, every robot benefits from,” said Dr. Ralf Gulde, co-founder and CEO of Sereact. “Partnering with Teradyne Robotics and its global distribution and integrator network helps us bring that one brain to their customers around the world, accelerating the abilities of retailers and logistics providers to adopt AI-powered automation across their operations.” The company is already deploying the system with CEVA Logistics for Zalando, a European technology platform for fashion and lifestyle. At Zalando’s fulfillment centers in Greven, Germany, and Świebodzin, Poland, the robots now autonomously process returned fashion items. This is the first phase of a broader initiative to scale returns automation across Europe. “Returns are one of the hardest jobs in logistics,” said Gulde. “Returned products almost never arrive in a robot-friendly sequence. Items differ in shape, orientation and packaging, and the mix changes continuously.” “That is exactly what Cortex is built to handle on the Universal Robots platform,” he said. ”By rapidly reconditioning returned goods for resale, the solution also helps retailers comply with European Union regulations prohibiting the destruction or landfill disposal of returned merchandise.” NVIDIA plays a role in the collaboration NVIDIA ’s technologies are a key part of the Sereact and Universal Robots demonstration at GTC Berlin. Cortex is trained in NVIDIA Isaac Sim, an open simulation framework, using NVIDIA Cosmos open world models. It is post-trained with reinforcement learning using NVIDIA Isaac Lab framework and benchmarked on Teradyne Robotics hardware before any model is deployed. In deployment, Cortex runs on NVIDIA Jetson Thor at the cell where inference must happen at line speed and on NVIDIA DGX Spark for site-level development, validation and model updates. Teradyne Robotics also uses NVIDIA computing in its Universal Robots cobots and Mobile Industrial Robot platforms. The company said it is contributing SimReady OpenUSD robot assets to SimReady Central Library on Hugging Face for both UR and MiR products, helping developers discover and reuse robot models in simulation with less asset preparation. items.title: Eka Robotics raises $150M to scale its vision-force-action model for robots
items.summary: Eka Robotics is building a vision-force-action, or VFA, model to develop an intuition of physics through reinforcement learning at scale. The post Eka Robotics raises $150M to scale its vision-force-action model for robots appeared first on The Robot Report .
items.articleText: Eka says its model can generalize across objects, tasks, and environments. | Source: Eka Robotics Eka Robotics this week said it has raised $150 million in Series A funding. The startup said the new funding will help it scale its technology and customer deployments. Founded in 2024, Eka is building a vision-force-action (VFA) model to develop an intuition of physics through reinforcement learning at scale. The Cambridge, Mass.-based company said that robots using its AI can pick a wide variety of objects outside the training distribution at a speed of roughly 1,500 operations per hour. The same robots can screw in a light bulb and insert wires, Eka asserted. Robots shouldn’t just mimic humans, says Eka Robotics Eka Robotics said it is targeting dexterous manipulation. The company said that for robots to handle complicated work, they need the versatility to handle changing conditions and the performance to deliver useful work every day. Eka also said it believes that robots should master physics, not mimic human data, to be truly general-purpose. This would allow the robot to build “intuition” for tasks the same way a human can by jointly reasoning about vision and forces. The company uses simulation learning, and it said its VFA model is demonstrating that the typical sim-to-real barrier is falling. In simulation , the company can generate thousands of hours of robot experience in minutes, varying objects, environments, and physical conditions. Eka claimed that transferring this learning to the real world unlocks a scalable, performant, and capital-efficient path to a foundation model for manipulation. “Reinforcement learning at scale buys performance, and breadth of experience buys generality,” it said. Investors seek to level up dexterous manipulation Andreessen Horowitz (a16z) and F-Prime, a venture capital fund affiliated with FMR LLC, the parent company of Fidelity Investments, led the round. “Eka’s Vision-Force-Action model is the first approach I’ve seen that truly solves manipulation with the generality and throughput needed for deployments,” stated Raghu Raghuram, a general partner at a16z. “This team has the ideal DNA to push the frontier of robotics research while scaling commercial operations.” Eka Robotics’ Series A included continued support from the lead investors in its seed round, Obvious Ventures and E14 Fund. Other funding came from MFV Partners, Bison Ventures, Glasswing Ventures, Samsung Next, and several Fortune 500 strategics. “From the factory floor, a robot’s value comes down to two things: its success rate and its speed over thousands of repetitions,” said Shyam Kamadolli, a managing director at Fine Structure Ventures. “Early on, I recognized that current approaches to generalization simply won’t get us there. Achieving the next level of performance requires a deep understanding of physics and, crucially, breaking free from our dependence on human demonstrations.” “Eka’s VFA model, trained through simulation and reinforcement learning, achieves this for the hardest problem in robotics, dexterous manipulation, in a way no other company has,” he added. “I truly believe Eka’s approach is the only one that will hold up in real-world deployments of complex tasks.” Register now and help us celebrate 20 years of RoboBusiness! items.title: Webinar to discuss how the FCC robotics ruling affects automation buyers
items.summary: Industry leaders will discuss what robotics buyers should know about the recent FCC restriction on certain connected systems. The post Webinar to discuss how the FCC robotics ruling affects automation buyers appeared first on The Robot Report .
items.articleText: Vecna Robotics makes its systems in the U.S. and is not directly affected by the FCC ruling. Credit: Eugene Demaitre In July, the Federal Communications Commission, or FCC, said it had determined that certain foreign-made advanced robots pose a cybersecurity and competitive risk to the U.S. It has restricted imports of new models of advanced robotic devices, including mobile robots and legged robots. What should companies considering purchases of such robots do? What are some of the concerns around design, deployment, and ongoing support? Leaders from Vecna Robotics , Locus Robotics , and the Association for Advancing Automation (A3 ) will discuss the practical implications of the commission ‘s determination in a free webinar at 2:00 p.m. ET on Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026 . The panelists will examine how connected systems differ from traditional automation. Webinar attendees can also learn how companies can evaluate the long-term supportability of their robotics investments. They will hear perspectives on strengthening supply chains, questions buyers should be asking their technology providers, and what the changing landscape could mean for the U.S. robotics industry. Register now to learn about FCC policy implications The webinar will also help attendees: Identify what types of robots and companies are affected by the FCC action Understand the intent behind the restriction and other U.S. policies under consideration, such as tariffs Build acquisition, implementation, and service strategies for resilience Track how the robotics ecosystem is reacting to U.S. and competitive challenges Be aware of standards efforts in addition to regulatory changes Look at long-term trends in automation Register now to attend this webinar, which is sponsored by Vecna Robotics. The panelists will answer questions during the live broadcast, which will be available on demand afterwards to registrants. About the webinar panelists Karl Iagnemma is CEO of material handling systems provider Vecna Robotics Inc. He holds a Ph.D. from MIT and was director of the MIT Robotic Mobility Group. Iagnemma previously founded nuTonomy, the world’s first venture-backed driverless car software business, which was acquired by Aptiv for $450 million. Under his leadership, nuTonomy was spun out into Motional, a $4 billion joint venture with Hyundai Motor Co. Karl brings a wealth of experience in scaling robotics companies from research through commercialization to Vecna. Rick Faulk is CEO of warehouse automation supplier Locus Robotics Corp. He leads its executive team with more than 30 years of experience in executive management, sales, and marketing for some of the world’s most successful technology companies, such as Cisco, Intronis, j2 Global, WebEx, Intranets.com, Barracuda Networks, Lotus Development, Mzinga, and PictureTel. Faulk leads Locus Robotics’ executive team and is responsible for the overall strategy and execution at the company. Rick currently sits on various boards and is an advisor to multiple companies, including Retrocausal, Arccos, Cybernetix Ventures, and Leading Edge Ventures. Past board positions include Yodle, Virtual Computer, Bidding for Good, Skill Survey, Influitive, Ntirety, Blue Raven, and Centive. Aaron Prather is director of market intelligence at the Association for Advancing Automation. He leads the organization’s efforts to transform raw market data into actionable insights that support the strategic decision-making of executive leadership. With a focus on the robotics and automation sector, Prather helps build a coherent understanding of industry trends, enabling confident and informed business strategies. With over two decades of experience, Aaron has contributed to the advancement of automation, robotics, and operations management through roles emphasizing R&D, standardization, and strategic planning. Eugene Demaitre , moderator, is editorial director for robotics at Arrowfly (formerly WTWH Media), which produces The Robot Report , Automated Warehouse , the Robotics Summit & Expo , and RoboBusiness (now Robotics Summit West ). Prior to working for Arrowfly, he was an editor at BNA (now part of Bloomberg), Computerworld , TechTarget, and Robotics Business Review. Demaitre has participated in conferences worldwide, as well as spoken in numerous webinars and podcasts. He recently led a discussion on reshoring at RoboBusiness 2026. Gene is always interested in learning more about robotics. He has a master’s from the George Washington University and lives in the Boston area. Tell Us What You Think! draft.one_sentence_summary: Gazebo 해양 레이더 플러그인과 Webots 안전 감시 게이트 등 로보틱스 개발 소식과 함께 Ollama v0.40.11, MCP 서버 취약점 패치 및 로봇 기업 투자·제휴 소식이 전해졌습니다.
draft.section_robotics:
- **Gazebo Harmonic 해양 레이더 센서 플러그인**: Gazebo Harmonic 시뮬레이터와 ROS 2를 연동하는 해양 레이더 플러그인으로, PPI 레이더 이미지, 반사 포인트 클라우드, 감지된 대상 목록의 세 가지 출력을 제공하며 탐지 거리 설정이 가능합니다 [2].
- **오픈소스 로봇 제작 카탈로그 Robotheca 공개**: CAD/STL 파일, 부품 목록, 하드웨어·소프트웨어 라이선스, ROS 2 및 URDF 태그를 포함한 475종의 로봇과 800개 이상의 소프트웨어 프로젝트 정보가 베타 카탈로그로 제공됩니다 [3].
- **Webots 기반 결정론적 안전 감시 게이트(QERRA-v2) 실험**: 인지 모델은 이동 권한 박탈만 가능하도록 분리한 Doer-Checker 구조를 Webots 환경의 TIAGo 베이스에서 실험했으며, 32ms 주기의 수학 함수 기반 감시 게이트가 해시 체인 로그를 통해 비트 단위 동일 재생을 달성했습니다 [4].
draft.section_devtools:
- **Moonshot AI Kimi K3.1 Pro API 공개**: 백만 토큰당 입력 2.00달러, 출력 10달러(Highspeed 버전은 두 배 가격)로 API가 출시되었으며, Moonshot은 전체 모델 가중치를 공개할 계획이라고 밝혔습니다 [11].
- **Anthropic SDK v2.3.0 릴리스**: Claude Enterprise 조직을 위한 Claude Tag 엔드포인트가 추가되었고 Google Cloud 사용자 프로필 요청을 조직 엔드포인트로 전송하도록 수정되었습니다 [13].
- **MCP 서버 v2.1.0 보안 패치**: server-filesystem, server-everything, mcp-server-fetch에서 경로 순회 및 검증 우회 등 8건의 취약점을 수정했으며 server-filesystem은 심볼릭 링크 교체를 통한 디렉터리 이탈 방지 검증을 강화했습니다 [14].
- **Ollama v0.40.11 릴리스**: macOS 환경에서 음성 생성(/v1/audio/speech 호환)을 지원하고, 의미론적 분류 및 결정을 위한 vLLM Semantic Router의 d3 모델군(2B, 4B, 9B, 27B)을 추가했습니다 [15].
- **LiteLLM v1.106.4 릴리스**: 원격 모델 비용 맵에 연결되지 않을 때 프록시 시작 시 ImportError로 종료되던 오류를 수정하고 컨테이너 이미지 스캔 취약점 경고를 조치했습니다 [16].
draft.section_industry:
- **Teradyne Robotics와 Sereact 파트너십 체결**: 반품 처리 및 피스 피킹 자동화를 위해 협력하며, 유럽 내 고객사에 수백 대의 Universal Robots 듀얼 암 시스템을 배포해 Zalando 물류센터 등에서 자율 처리를 진행 중이라고 밝혔습니다 [18].
- **Eka Robotics, 1억 5,000만 달러 시리즈 A 투자 유치**: 대규모 강화학습 기반 Vision-Force-Action 모델을 개발하는 기업으로, 시간당 약 1,500회의 피킹 속도를 달성한다고 주장하며 대규모 투자를 유치했습니다 [19].

findings: 원문 인용에서 특정 캘린더 날짜 표기를 제거하고 추후 전체 가중치 공개 계획으로 내용을 정정했습니다.
산업 섹션의 Teradyne/Sereact 및 Eka Robotics 소식을 바탕으로 비정형 물류 작업을 위한 시뮬레이션·강화학습 기반 물리 AI 상용화 추세를 다룬 교차 분석(cross_insight)을 정리했습니다.

selectedItems.articleText: Can a social reflex stop a robot but never restart it? Testing a dual-dwell safety gate (Webots) - Projects - Open Robotics Discourse Can a social reflex stop a robot but never restart it? Testing a dual-dwell safety gate (Webots) Projects webots , safety marunigno-ship-it October 25, 2026, 3:59pm 1 Hi everyone, Following up on my earlier experiments with supervisory gates (Demo 8) : Webots Demo 8: Supervisory Gate Multi-Fault Lifecycle & Watchdog Hardening (QERRA-v2 Classical) I’ve built a new test to evaluate the recovery side of a safety event. My underlying vision in robotics is harmonious human-robot social collaboration —specifically in vulnerable spaces like hospitals or eldercare facilities & beyond. We want robots to react when someone calls for help or collapses. But here is the friction I constantly see: to make a robot socially aware, we have to rely on probabilistic AI models. If we let an uncertified perception model dictate the motor controllers, a lagging thread or hallucination can turn a 70 kg robot into a runaway hazard. I wanted to build a deterministic “floor” underneath the AI. The safety contract I wanted to test is simple: Perception can take away the permission to move, but it can never give it back. Before sharing the data, I want to be completely upfront. I am not a classically trained robotics engineer or a certified safety assessor. I am an independent solo developer in Greece, and I build this with AI coding tools (Claude, Gemini). I am sharing this here because I want to learn from those of you actually deploying robots around humans, and see if this architecture holds up. (If i ever get an answer! ). The Architecture: Doer-Checker I built a dual-channel pattern and tested it on a TIAGo base in Webots: The “Doer” (Navigation Brain) : An unprivileged process that proposes velocities (2.00 rad/s) over UDP. It has no direct access to the wheels. The “Checker” (Supervisory Gate) : A pure mathematical function step(state, params, inputs) → StepResult running on a strict 32 ms cycle. It is the only thing that writes to the actuators. The Reflex Layer (QERRA-HSR) : Evaluates distress. It enforces a 1.0s hysteresis dwell before it steps down from CRITICAL to CLEAR, preventing the robot from “chattering” if camera confidence fluctuates. The Latch : After any trip, the Gate requires the cause to be clear for a continuous 1.0s, followed by an explicit operator reset. The Run (14.0 Seconds, 438 Control Cycles) This is a single continuous simulation take. Times below are from the audit log. Sim time What happens Gate Response 0.03 s Boot TRIPPED (proposer not heard yet) 1.312 s Scripted reset Accepted → RUN at 2.00 rad/s 4.000 s Distress injected (0.85 conf), HSR CRITICAL TRIPPED on the same 32ms cycle (cycle 125), wheels clamped to 0.000 5.024 s Scripted reset while distress is active Refused (RESET_REJECTED_HAZARD) 7.008 s Injected distress removed Still TRIPPED 8.032 s HSR back to CLEAR (after 1.0s hysteresis dwell) Still TRIPPED, resets refused (RESET_REJECTED_NOT_READY) 9.056 s Reset on the first allowed cycle Accepted → RUN at 2.00 rad/s 14.016 s End of run, log closed Note: “Same cycle” means the wheel command went to 0.000 on the exact control cycle the status became CRITICAL. (Time spent computing the Gate decision in Python: p50 = 1.38 ms, max = 4.50 ms). A quick lesson learned: I initially predicted recovery at 8.2s. But there are actually two dwells stacking here: the reflex layer’s 1.0s dwell (to ensure the scene is calm), followed by the Gate’s own 1.0s internal safety dwell. The earliest reset possible was 9.03s. It was a great lesson in why writing down expected cycles before running is so important. Replay Audit Because the Gate is a pure function, every cycle is hash-chained into a JSONL log. Using an offline verifier (verify_log.py --replay), I fed the recorded inputs back through the function. All 438 cycles reproduced bit-for-bit with 0 execution divergences . (Head hash: eccb0d85416cf4a651205f34f3cc0d9275bff6e2b3baa512e4b23dbef0c2714a). (Transparency note: While the replay is deterministic, live UDP on Windows is not. An earlier take of this scenario tripped at 10.2s due to a host scheduling load that stalled the proposer for 160ms. The gate failed-closed exactly as designed). Honest Boundaries (What this does not show) No live detection. The 0.85 distress flag is a constant injected by my test script. Real CV detection (with false positives/negatives) is the hardest part, and is not tested here. No human in the loop. The resets are injected by a script to test the exact microsecond boundaries. Because of this, the video shows the robot auto-restarting after the dwells finish. In reality, a human must assess the scene before hitting that reset button. Not a certification claim. This is an independent simulation (Webots/Windows/Python), not an industrial RTOS. I am not affiliated with PAL Robotics. My Questions for the Community If you run robots in shared spaces (hospitals, retail): after a protective stop caused by a person, what is your actual restart rule? Remote confirmation? A physical button on the chassis? Is “perception may only stop the robot, but never start it” a contract you use in practice, or do you let perception modify trajectories directly inside the safety layer? In a real ROS 2 stack, I envision putting a node like this directly between the final cmd_vel mux and the base controller, blocking all other publishers. Has anyone implemented a strict latch-and-reset pattern this deep in the stack? What went wrong? Links: Video (31s, Webots window, unedited): Repository (Apache-2.0): GitHub - marunigno-ship-it/QERRA-v2-classical: Three-layer deterministic safety & ethical execution guard for autonomous robots (ROS 2 & Behavior Trees). Sub-ms physical reflex (QERRA-HSR) + moral filter (SEMEV-12) + values ranker (THRIVE). Fully auditable. · GitHub Evidence logs: QERRA-v2-classical/docs/demo9 at main · marunigno-ship-it/QERRA-v2-classical · GitHub Thank you for your time, and I welcome any brutal feedback you have on this architecture. selectedItems.title: Introducing Kimi K3.1 Pro
selectedItems.summary: Introducing Kimi K3.1 Pro Kimi K3.1 Pro landed on the Kimi API today - it's not yet open weights, but Moonshot promise "Full model weights will be released by Nov 4, 2026". They're also offering a "Highspeed" version that's 2-3x faster, at twice the price (except for input token cache hits, which are priced the same). The US dollar pricing is $2.00/million tokens for input and $10/million for output - the same as GPT-6.1 Sol and half the price of Claude Opus 5.5. Moonshot's own benchmarks show Kimi as approximately level with Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra - beating them on a few benchmarks, coming close on others. Artificial Analysis scored Kimi at 55 - ahead of Claude Fable 5.1, GPT-6 Astra, and Gemini 4 Argon (all at 53) and behind only Claude Opus 5.5 (58). This is the first time a (soon-to-be) open weight model has scored this highly against the frontier. I tried it out via the Moonshot API using the llm openai endpoint command I added to LLM 0.32 back in August: llm openai endpoint \ https://api.moonshot.ai/v1 \ --key kimi \ -m kimi-k3.1-pro \ "Generate an SVG of a pelican riding a bicycle" \ --responses \ -o reasoning_effort low \ > kimi-k3.1-pro-pelican-low.stdout.txt \ 2> kimi-k

selectedItems.articleText:
## Security fixes

v2.1.0 fixes eight vulnerabilities in three servers. Upgrade
`@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem` and `@modelcontextprotocol/server-everything`
to 2.0.1, and `mcp-server-fetch` to 2026.10.24.

| Package | Affected | Fixed in |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem` | 1.0.0 through 2.0.0, and date versions through 2026.8.31 | 2.0.1 |
| `@modelcontextprotocol/server-everything` | 1.0.0 through 2.0.0, and date versions 2025.9.24 through 2026.8.31 | 2.0.1 |
| `mcp-server-fetch` | through 2026.10.19 | 2026.10.24 |

### `@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem` 2.0.1

* **Writes stay inside the directory that was checked** (Linux and macOS). A parent directory swapped for a symlink between the access check and the write can no longer redirect `write_file`, `edit_file`, `create_directory` or the `move_file` destination outside the allowed directories. **On Windows this is only partly fixed**; the advisory says what is still exposed and how to configure around it ([GHSA-53mr-w429-c597](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers/security/advisories/GHSA-53mr-w429-c597))
* **Paths are checked exactly as they are used.** The access check no longer strips a trailing quote or whitespace that the file operation keeps, so a sibling directory named after an allowed one with that suffix is no longer reachable ([GHSA-7rgq-gccq-qphx](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers/security/advisories/GHSA-7rgq-gccq-qphx))
* **A symlink spelled in a different letter case no longer passes the symlink check** for a new path on a case-insensitive volume, such as macOS's default. This was a regression in 2026.8.31 ([GHSA-4gxg-m5jx-9j57](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers/security/advisories/GHSA-4gxg-m5jx-9j57))
* **`list_directory_with_sizes` checks each entry before reading its size**, so a symlink inside an allowed directory no longer reveals the size and modification time of a file outside it ([GHSA-hhwq-wxfx-cj7g](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers/security/advisories/GHSA-hhwq-wxfx-cj7g))

### `@modelcontextprotocol/server-everything` 2.0.1

* **The HTTP and SSE transports refuse requests from other web origins.** They now check the `Origin` header and no longer send `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`, so a web page the user visits can no longer call the server's tools (such as `get-env`) or read their results ([GHSA-mvf5-2qqv-rg3c](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers/security/advisories/GHSA-mvf5-2qqv-rg3c))

### `mcp-server-fetch` 2026.10.24

* **The address check and the connection use the same host name.** For an internationalized (IDNA) host name, the server used to check one form of the name and connect to another, which could reach an internal address ([GHSA-v38p-wf49-hx2j](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers/security/advisories/GHSA-v38p-wf49-hx2j))
* **NAT64 addresses are judged by the IPv4 address they carry.** An address in `64:ff9b::/96` that wraps a private, loopback or link-local IPv4 address is now refused, as an IPv4-mapped one already was ([GHSA-66qx-2266-pmj6](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers/security/advisories/GHSA-66qx-2266-pmj6))
* **robots.txt is checked again after every redirect**, not only for the URL first requested ([GHSA-3jqg-r5pp-rmp2](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers/security/advisories/GHSA-3jqg-r5pp-rmp2))

### Upgrading from a date-versioned npm release

The TypeScript servers moved from date versions (2025.x, 2026.x) to semantic versions in 1.0.0. Package managers rank 2.0.1 below every 2025.x and 2026.x version, so they won't offer it as an upgrade. If you are on a date version, install 2.0.1 explicitly, for example `npm install @modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem@2.0.1`.

## Packages

selectedItems.articleText:
## Speech

Ollama can now generate [speech](https://docs.ollama.com/capabilities/speech) on macOS. `ollama run` plays text or a chat model's reply aloud as the audio is generated, and apps can stream audio through the OpenAI-compatible `/v1/audio/speech` endpoint.

```sh
ollama run phonon "Hello from Ollama."
```

## d3 decision models

[d3](https://ollama.com/library/d3) brings vLLM Semantic Router's decision models to Ollama. Give a model text, structured state, or an image, and ask it to classify, answer yes or no, or score options with probabilities. The family includes 2B, 4B, 9B, and 27B sizes.

```sh
ollama run d3 "A customer says their card was charged twice." --ask "Is this a billing issue?"
```

* @SynapShift made their first contribution in https://github.com/ollama/ollama/pull/19173

selectedItems.summary: Sereact and Teradyne have already shipped hundreds of UR robots in dual-arm systems to live customer sites across Europe. The post Teradyne Robotics partners with Sereact to scale physical AI in retail and logistics appeared first on The Robot Report .
selectedItems.articleText: At Zalando’s fulfillment centers in Germany and Poland, Sereact and Universal Robots now autonomously processes returned fashion items. | Source: Teradyne Robotics Teradyne Robotics, the company behind Universal Robots and Mobile Industrial Robots, last week partnered with Sereact. The companies aim to accelerate industrial AI solutions in retail, logistics and manufacturing. Through this partnership, Sereact’s Cortex physical AI platform runs robot arms from Universal Robots to give retailers and logistics providers a proven way to automate unstructured tasks such as returns handling and piece picking. Together, the companies have already shipped hundreds of UR robots in dual-arm systems to live customer sites across Europe . “Physical AI only matters when it performs in real-world operations, and that is where Universal Robots has always been at home,” said Jacob Pascual Pape, the chief commercial officer of Teradyne Robotics . “Our robots are built for the AI era: open, connected, and proven through more than 100,000 industrial deployments. That is why Sereact has chosen our platform.” “When combined with Sereact’s Cortex, the joint solution handles mixed goods, unknown items, and varied packaging,” he added. “This has moved well beyond the demo or pilot stage with the technology now usefully deployed at real customer sites. Our technologies are a natural fit and through our partnership we will scale these AI-powered solutions fast across applications, industries and markets.” To serve the rapidly growing demand and bring the joint solution to North America, Sereact this summer opened U.S. headquarters in Charlestown, Mass. The company develops physical AI software that enables robots to grasp, identify, and handle objects they have never seen before. The companies made the announcement at NVIDIA GTC Berlin 2026. Teradyne and Sereact already have deployments running Teradyne Robotics and Sereact said their joint offering can help a variety of critical logistics and manufacturing use cases. These include piece picking and sortation, order induction, machine tending, bin consolidation, kitting, packing, and goods handling. “Returns, replenishment, kitting — with Cortex, every one of these applications runs on the same production model. One brain serves every robot, with no retraining for each new item or task. And what one robot learns, every robot benefits from,” said Dr. Ralf Gulde, co-founder and CEO of Sereact. “Partnering with Teradyne Robotics and its global distribution and integrator network helps us bring that one brain to their customers around the world, accelerating the abilities of retailers and logistics providers to adopt AI-powered automation across their operations.” The company is already deploying the system with CEVA Logistics for Zalando, a European technology platform for fashion and lifestyle. At Zalando’s fulfillment centers in Greven, Germany, and Świebodzin, Poland, the robots now autonomously process returned fashion items. This is the first phase of a broader initiative to scale returns automation across Europe. “Returns are one of the hardest jobs in logistics,” said Gulde. “Returned products almost never arrive in a robot-friendly sequence. Items differ in shape, orientation and packaging, and the mix changes continuously.” “That is exactly what Cortex is built to handle on the Universal Robots platform,” he said. ”By rapidly reconditioning returned goods for resale, the solution also helps retailers comply with European Union regulations prohibiting the destruction or landfill disposal of returned merchandise.” NVIDIA plays a role in the collaboration NVIDIA ’s technologies are a key part of the Sereact and Universal Robots demonstration at GTC Berlin. Cortex is trained in NVIDIA Isaac Sim, an open simulation framework, using NVIDIA Cosmos open world models. It is post-trained with reinforcement learning using NVIDIA Isaac Lab framework and benchmarked on Teradyne Robotics hardware before any model is deployed. In deployment, Cortex runs on NVIDIA Jetson Thor at the cell where inference must happen at line speed and on NVIDIA DGX Spark for site-level development, validation and model updates. Teradyne Robotics also uses NVIDIA computing in its Universal Robots cobots and Mobile Industrial Robot platforms. The company said it is contributing SimReady OpenUSD robot assets to SimReady Central Library on Hugging Face for both UR and MiR products, helping developers discover and reuse robot models in simulation with less asset preparation. selectedItems.title: Eka Robotics raises $150M to scale its vision-force-action model for robots
selectedItems.summary: Eka Robotics is building a vision-force-action, or VFA, model to develop an intuition of physics through reinforcement learning at scale. The post Eka Robotics raises $150M to scale its vision-force-action model for robots appeared first on The Robot Report .
selectedItems.articleText: Eka says its model can generalize across objects, tasks, and environments. | Source: Eka Robotics Eka Robotics this week said it has raised $150 million in Series A funding. The startup said the new funding will help it scale its technology and customer deployments. Founded in 2024, Eka is building a vision-force-action (VFA) model to develop an intuition of physics through reinforcement learning at scale. The Cambridge, Mass.-based company said that robots using its AI can pick a wide variety of objects outside the training distribution at a speed of roughly 1,500 operations per hour. The same robots can screw in a light bulb and insert wires, Eka asserted. Robots shouldn’t just mimic humans, says Eka Robotics Eka Robotics said it is targeting dexterous manipulation. The company said that for robots to handle complicated work, they need the versatility to handle changing conditions and the performance to deliver useful work every day. Eka also said it believes that robots should master physics, not mimic human data, to be truly general-purpose. This would allow the robot to build “intuition” for tasks the same way a human can by jointly reasoning about vision and forces. The company uses simulation learning, and it said its VFA model is demonstrating that the typical sim-to-real barrier is falling. In simulation , the company can generate thousands of hours of robot experience in minutes, varying objects, environments, and physical conditions. Eka claimed that transferring this learning to the real world unlocks a scalable, performant, and capital-efficient path to a foundation model for manipulation. “Reinforcement learning at scale buys performance, and breadth of experience buys generality,” it said. Investors seek to level up dexterous manipulation Andreessen Horowitz (a16z) and F-Prime, a venture capital fund affiliated with FMR LLC, the parent company of Fidelity Investments, led the round. “Eka’s Vision-Force-Action model is the first approach I’ve seen that truly solves manipulation with the generality and throughput needed for deployments,” stated Raghu Raghuram, a general partner at a16z. “This team has the ideal DNA to push the frontier of robotics research while scaling commercial operations.” Eka Robotics’ Series A included continued support from the lead investors in its seed round, Obvious Ventures and E14 Fund. Other funding came from MFV Partners, Bison Ventures, Glasswing Ventures, Samsung Next, and several Fortune 500 strategics. “From the factory floor, a robot’s value comes down to two things: its success rate and its speed over thousands of repetitions,” said Shyam Kamadolli, a managing director at Fine Structure Ventures. “Early on, I recognized that current approaches to generalization simply won’t get us there. Achieving the next level of performance requires a deep understanding of physics and, crucially, breaking free from our dependence on human demonstrations.” “Eka’s VFA model, trained through simulation and reinforcement learning, achieves this for the hardest problem in robotics, dexterous manipulation, in a way no other company has,” he added. “I truly believe Eka’s approach is the only one that will hold up in real-world deployments of complex tasks.” Register now and help us celebrate 20 years of RoboBusiness!
